title: Tansy and the Sunpetal Secret
markdown:
The Whisperwind Peaks kept mist the way some houses keep cats: curled, proprietary, occasionally blocking the door. When the moon was only a sliver, the vapour lay along the ridges like dragons who had agreed to nap. Bells travelled from stone to stone. The air hummed with leftover tales. In a valley cradled by pines whose needles sighed on purpose, Tansy catalogued rare mosses, brow furrowed, and polished her spectacles with a lint-free cloth until they behaved like captured stars. She was not a cackling, cauldron-theatrics sort of witch. Her most constant companion was Wisp, a snow hare of almost unreasonable quiet. His fur, so white it seemed spun from moonlight, shifted toward the dappled grey of granite as the seasons turned, a silent echo of the ground. His twitching nose sorted approaching storms from wild strawberries from, crucially, nonsense.

The errand, on paper, was simple. A jar of Sunpetal Honey from the market in Whispering Gulch, without which her famous Sleepytime Tea could not negotiate with a disgruntled mountain troll who had stubbed a toe. Everyone in the valley knew the tea. Everyone also knew that simple errands, nestled among mist and echo, rarely stayed simple. They unfurled, like fern in spring, whether you had asked them to or not.

“Sunpetal Honey,” Tansy told Wisp, buckling the satchel. “A hop, skip, and a jump.”

Wisp’s ear disagreed, politely.

The first obstruction appeared in the usual place: the chasm. Piran the ferryman, a man whose beard was perpetually tangled with cobwebs and the faint scent of river reeds, would not take Tansy to Whispering Gulch without a little local custom. Recite a particularly knotty riddle backwards. Toss three perfectly round pebbles into the churning silver gorge. Balance on one leg while doing both, a feat that would have made an acrobatic pixie file paperwork.

“I need to get across,” Tansy said. “The market is nine. These pebbles, Piran, are delightfully irregular. Almost lumpy.”

Piran’s grin showed a democracy of teeth. “Tradition. The mist respects the old ways. It will not part for a hurried witch.”

Tansy, ever observant, noticed a faint almost imperceptible shimmer in the mist just beyond Piran’s hand, a place where his voice seemed to fade as if the vapour had an appetite. She also noticed Wisp, quietly watching from under a patch of particularly resilient mountain thyme, nudging a smooth flat grey stone to her feet. “Thank you, Wisp. A flat stone. How very precise.” She declined the lumpy pebbles with politeness that did not invite debate. She tossed her own river stone, collected on a less complicated errand. It spun with uncalled-for grace. The mist did not clear in the dramatic way of a grand Rite. A small quiet eddy formed, a swirl that parted vapour just enough for the rickety rope ferry, Piran at the helm, to glide. His jaw nearly unhinged. Then a shrug rippled the beard.

“Never seen that. Mist being particularly accommodating. Rare.”

“Patience,” Tansy murmured, grandmother’s sentence, not a slogan. “All in time.”

Next necessary stop: Ignis Spectaculus, the dragon who kept the highest, least sociable peak, a king among crags and, more importantly, among spectacles. He was renowned not only for wisdom but for lenses that gleamed in light that had not been invited. Emerald scales, a thousand of them. Eyes like libraries behind glass. He regarded Tansy as tectonic plates regard a polite knock.

“Ah, Tansy. An errand. The valley’s rhythms complicate a cup of tea. A bit like catching a butterfly with a fishing net.” He adjusted the spectacles with a claw the size of Tansy’s head, and did it as if the frames were china. “For Sunpetal Honey you will need, as always, a vessel of patience and a tool for discerning truth. I have just the thing.”

A flick of tail sent ripples through the air and a small carved wooden spoon toward her boots. Ordinary, at first. The handle was a tiny feather, so fine it seemed nearly alive. “Spoon of Unvarnished Essence. It shows the true nature of what it touches, or stirs. Use it wisely. And with a clear heart.”

Tansy thanked him. Quiet amusement lived at the corner of her mouth. She turned the smooth wood in her palm. “How practical.” Delight, rare and exact.

A rather lengthy detour to admire luminous fungi — Wisp had pointed with the authority of a nose — and then the market of Whispering Gulch, which was less a market than an argument conducted in colour. Stalls overflowed with silks that whispered, trinkets that clanked their own tunes, and goblin spices pungent enough to tickle a feud. Rattlegrub, ears drooping like wilted ferns, nose hunting opportunity, was the sole purveyor of Sunpetal Honey. He sat behind a precarious mound of jars, beady eyes assessing wallets.

“Sunpetal Honey. A quart.”

He cackled, a handful of dry pebbles in a tin, and Wisp’s ears went flat. “Finest, most potent, gathered this morn.” He rummaged with jerky excitement and produced a jar that was not glowing gold. It was thick, murky, dark, pulsing with a faint sickly green, swamp-gas in glass.

“Pure unadulterated Glow-Worm Goo. Guaranteed to make you see in the darkest cave.”

Tansy’s noticing did its job without being asked. Colour wrong. Pulse unpleasant. Wisp, who had observed from a distance that counted as diplomacy, let out a soft chatter of clicks and nudged the satchel, then the shin. Look closer. Amiss.

“Glow-worm goo,” she said. “And I require honey. If you are going to be mysterious, you could at least be punctual with the deception.”

The spoon went in. Instantly the green flared like a startled firefly. The wood took the same illness, undeniable. “Ah. So it is. Quite potent, I am sure.”

Rattlegrub’s mouth hung like a half-opened clamshell. Tansy stirred with the sort of deliberation that makes air pay attention. The intense green thinned. The muddy pulse shimmered, condensed, coalesced as if drawn, and became not goo but a small perfectly formed luminous drop of golden honey, concentrated, warm enough to argue with the market’s gloom. The stalls held their breath. Wisp hopped forward without sound and nudged the drop; it pulsed, as if pleased to have been found out.

Tansy collected it with reverence into her clean jar. “The spoon does not invent, Rattlegrub. It strips the extra. Your goo, once unvarnished, had a more honest occupation underneath. Excellent for caves, or lost bats. Useless in Sleepytime Tea until now.”

Rattlegrub, after a silence as long as a winter evening, let out a surprisingly hearty laugh, less tin, more person. He wiped an eye. “Well, I’ll be a mushroom’s uncle. The dragon’s spoon. Fancy that.” He straightened his tunic. A new glint. “A quart of concentrated Sunpetal Essence, then. You’ve paid in a way more interesting, and frankly more honest, than coin. A good chuckle. A lesson.”

As Tansy left, jar ticking warmth against her hip, the valley air felt lighter, sweeter. The sun, higher now, had the same temperature as the honey. Wisp trotted, fur white as the high remaining snow, nose busy with the ordinary. She did not explain the valley. Behind them the ferry rope creaked, Piran presumably still crediting the mist. The drop in the glass was a small unvarnished fact on the walk home, and the market, behind, had already begun to invent three versions of what it had seen.
characters: Tansy (witch who catalogs rare mosses), Wisp (a snow hare who senses approaching nonsense), Ignis Spectaculus (a dragon who polishes enormous spectacles)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for teens
